items.stem: In Haskell, why is the IO type needed for reading input or printing output?

options.text: It keeps effects explicit in the type system and lets the pure core stay referentially transparent while effects run at the edges
options.rationale: Correct: IO marks effectful computations so purity is preserved and effects are sequenced explicitly.

options.text: It makes the program run faster by caching results
options.rationale: IO is about modelling effects, not caching or speed.

options.text: It is required for any arithmetic operation

items.explanation: Correct: IO marks effectful computations so purity is preserved and effects are sequenced explicitly.
items.domain_ref: Working with IO and the Maybe and Either types

items.stem: Which statements about Haskell type classes are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: A type class defines a set of functions that instance types must implement
options.rationale: Correct: a type class specifies an interface that each instance provides.

options.text: They enable ad-hoc polymorphism so one function name works across many types
options.rationale: Correct: type classes give overloaded behaviour resolved by the type.

options.text: A type can belong to at most one type class
options.rationale: A type can be an instance of many type classes.

options.text: Type class methods are dispatched on a runtime object header like OOP virtual methods
options.rationale: Dispatch is resolved by type, typically at compile time, not via a runtime object header.

items.explanation: Correct: a type class specifies an interface that each instance provides.; Correct: type classes give overloaded behaviour resolved by the type.
items.domain_ref: Types, type classes and type inference

items.stem: What does laziness allow you to do with an expression like take 5 [1..] ?

options.text: Produce only the elements that are demanded, so an infinite list can be used safely
options.rationale: Correct: lazy evaluation computes values only as needed, so take 5 forces just five elements.

options.text: Evaluate the whole infinite list first and then slice it
options.rationale: That would never terminate; laziness avoids forcing the whole list.

options.text: Convert the list into a strict array in memory
options.rationale: Laziness avoids building the full structure, not forces it.

options.text: Run the computation on multiple cores automatically
options.rationale: Laziness is about evaluation order, not parallelism.

items.explanation: Correct: lazy evaluation computes values only as needed, so take 5 forces just five elements.
